scenes.contextualRelevance: The video discusses the use of the publicly accessible surface web for clandestine activities, challenging the perception that these activities solely belong to the deep web.

narrativeProgression.description: Brian J. Frederick introduces the concept of the surface web, deep web, and dark web.
He expresses particular interest in how the surface web is used in dark ways.
He gives examples of webcam applications like Skype, Zoom, UvU, and TeamViewer, where people can share drug experiences anonymously.
He highlights the invite-only nature of these platforms, making tracking activities difficult.
He suggests that these activities could be considered part of the deep web, but he prefers to classify them as the surface web.
He argues that these platforms are publicly accessible but used clandestinely.
He mentions Grinder, a platform with a large user base, where people share links to their Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram accounts.
He emphasizes the ability to track individuals' activities across different platforms.
He introduces Google Reverse Image Search as a tool to identify individuals based on their photos.
He concludes by questioning the perception of anonymity online and highlighting the need to address the issue of traceability.

scenes.thematicElements: The video explores themes such as the illusion of anonymity on the internet, traceability in the digital age, and the blurred lines between surface web and deep web.

text_to_speech: There is the surface web, there is the deep web and there is the dark net. What I am particularly interested in is the surface web, how it’s used in dark ways for instance using technology such as Skype, Zoom, ooVoo, TeamViewer. These web cam applications where individuals can share drug experiences, but you are not necessarily able to track their activities, because they are invite-only platforms. You could call that the deep web if you like, but I personally like to think it’s the surface web, because it is kind of up there on the top, but it is used in a clandestine kind of way, where you have networks of 2 to 25 and more individuals performing drug experiences together, but there is no URL address to go to, there is no website to go to. You are invited, if you are not invited, you don’t have access to this environment. What I am seeing a lot of is, for instance, with Grindr, which is a 6-million-member maybe more audience now, there will be links to a person’s Facebook account or links to a Twitter account, there may be links to an Instagram account. And you can track the activities of these men across the different networks that they belong to. You can even use, for instance, Google reverse image search. The photograph of an individual’s face, if you upload it into Google reverse image search, now you can find their Facebook page, their Instagram, if they have that same photo uploaded. This perception of anonymity really needs to be addressed. These individuals don’t know that they are actually traceable through the images they are putting up.

youtube_description:
Interview with Brian J. Frederick, one of the authors of 'The internet and drug markets': http://www.emcdda.europa.eu/publications/insights/internet-drug-markets

The last decade has seen the emergence of new internet technologies that have acted as important facilitators of online drug markets. The internet now hosts a range of virtual marketplaces (both on the surface and deep web) for selling and buying illicit substances, as well as representing a new arena for health and law enforcement interventions. This first EMCDDA investigation into the world of online drug markets brings together state-of-the-art input from over 20 experts — from academia, journalism and frontline practice — and contributes to the knowledge base on this part of the supply chain.

Music: Alessandro Pirona.
